__comment: NVisionX Services Detail — merges the platform-service dashboards (Content Service runtime, Credential Manager, Knowledge Hub [sidecar+standalone], Knowledge Service, Registration Service, Request Service, Backend Workers/Archiver/Archiver v2/Enricher - 13 files total) into one file, one collapsed row per service, each repeating per client via the shared Clients picker. Same pattern and same trade-offs as connectors-detail.json (namespace hardcoded to default, per-pod filters dropped to wildcards since they can't cascade correctly under row-repeat). 2026-09-18: built alongside Connectors Detail per manager request for ~8-10 total dashboards, each client-selectable.

options.content:
**Services Detail** — one section per platform service, each repeating once per client selected in the **Clients** picker (top of page). Expand a service's row to see its full golden-signal, domain-metric, and runtime detail for the selected client(s).

**Note:** as with Connectors Detail, this view aggregates rather than offering a per-pod filter picker - Grafana can't cascade a chained variable correctly once a row repeats per client.

panels.title: Process CPU (rate)
panels.description: CPU seconds burned per second, per pod. 1.0 means one core fully occupied. Read this against the container CPU limit on the row below rather than against the node: extraction runs many documents at once per pod (EXTRACTION_MAX_CONCURRENCY in the applications chart), so a pod can want far more CPU than it is allowed and the excess shows up as throttling, not as a higher line here.

panels.title: Process Resident Memory
panels.description: RSS as the kernel sees it. This is the number that gets compared with the container memory limit by the OOM killer, and it includes what the Go runtime has not yet returned to the OS — so it sits above heap in-use and falls more slowly.

panels.title: Process Virtual Memory
panels.description: Address space reserved, not memory used. Go reserves large arenas up front, so this is normally flat, large, and uninteresting — it is here to distinguish a genuine allocation climb (resident rises with it) from an address-space artefact (only this rises).

panels.title: Container CPU vs limit
panels.description: cgroup CPU usage against the configured limit. The limit is plotted from kube-state-metrics rather than drawn as a fixed threshold, so it follows a helm change on the next rollout instead of going stale — the value itself lives in contentService.resources in the applications chart. Requests and limits are set equal for this service, so there is no burst headroom above the line.

panels.title: Container Memory (working set) vs limit
panels.description: Working set against the memory limit — the pair the OOM killer acts on. Worth watching closely here, because the two limits are not treated alike: the runtime sizes GOMAXPROCS from the cgroup CPU quota on its own, but nothing does the same for memory — GOMEMLIMIT defaults to unlimited and neither the binary nor the chart sets it, so the GC will grow the heap toward the cgroup ceiling without ever knowing it is there. A whole document is held in memory while it is extracted and compressed, so headroom is consumed by document size times concurrency, not by steady-state load. Requests equal limits for this service, so the limit line is also the guaranteed allocation.

panels.title: CPU throttling (share of periods)
panels.description: Fraction of CFS periods in which the container was throttled. Anything sustained above zero means the pod is being held below the CPU it is asking for, which lengthens every latency panel on the other content-service dashboards without producing a single error. Expect this to be the first thing that moves when extraction concurrency is raised.

targets.expr: sum by (pod) (rate(container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total{namespace="default", pod=~".*content-service.*", container="content-service"}[5m])) / clamp_min(sum by (pod) (rate(container_cpu_cfs_periods_total{namespace="default", pod=~".*content-service.*", container="content-service"}[5m])), 1)

panels.title: Goroutines
panels.description: Goroutine count tracks in-flight work: NATS handlers, both gRPC servers, upload streams and every admitted extraction hold goroutines. It should rise with load and come back to the same floor afterwards. A floor that steps up after each load period and never returns is the leak signal — an extraction that outlived its caller, or a stream that was never closed.

panels.title: Heap In-Use
panels.description: Live heap. Compare its shape with resident memory on the row above: heap that falls while RSS stays high is memory the runtime is holding rather than leaking, whereas both climbing together is the path to an OOM kill.

panels.title: GC Pause (max)
panels.description: Longest stop-the-world GC pause per pod. go_gc_duration_seconds is a Prometheus summary, not a histogram: there is no _bucket series, so histogram_quantile cannot be used here. The Go collector exposes quantiles 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 and 1 only — there is no 0.99. quantile="1" is the max pause over the runtime's buffer of recent GC cycles, so it reports the worst recent pause rather than a windowed percentile.

panels.title: GOMAXPROCS vs CPU limit
panels.description: How many OS threads the Go scheduler will run in parallel, against how much CPU the cgroup actually allows. The module is on go 1.26, so the runtime reads the cgroup CPU quota itself and re-checks it periodically: GOMAXPROCS should sit at the CPU limit rounded up and follow a limit change without a restart. Divergence is the finding. A line pinned to the node core count instead means the container-aware default was switched off (GODEBUG containermaxprocs=0, or an explicit GOMAXPROCS env var), and the scheduler is then sizing itself for a machine far larger than the slice the pod owns — which turns into throttling on the row above rather than into more work done. The two series measure different things (threads against cores) and are plotted together only because the gap between them is the point.

panels.title: Open vs Max FDs
panels.description: Every S3 call, NATS connection, inbound gRPC stream and connector transfer holds a descriptor, so this is the real ceiling on concurrent work per pod. The gap between the two lines is the headroom; open climbing toward max while throughput is flat means descriptors are not being released.

panels.title: OS Threads
panels.description: Threads the runtime has created. Blocking syscalls — S3 reads, compression, extractor calls — each pin a thread for their duration, so this rises above GOMAXPROCS under load. A ratchet that never comes down usually means threads parked in blocking calls that are not completing.

panels.title: Pods scraped (fleet size)
panels.description: How many content-service pods Prometheus is currently scraping. This deployment is KEDA scaled, so the count moves on its own: scale-up appears here and as new series everywhere else on this dashboard, and it is not a restart. Read the per-pod panels above against this — a fleet sum such as extraction slots in use only makes sense divided by the number of pods reporting.

panels.title: Process Uptime
panels.description: Time since process start. Shutdown here is deliberately slow — the drain budget and the pod's termination grace period are both sized for the longest extraction that can still be running when SIGTERM lands (shutdownTimeoutSeconds and terminationGracePeriodSeconds in the applications chart) — so a rolling update shows a long overlap of old and new pods rather than a clean swap. A sawtooth with a short period is a crash loop, not a deploy.

panels.title: Container Restarts (1h increase)
panels.description: Restarts of the container inside an existing pod. KEDA replacing pods does not appear here — that is the fleet-size panel — so anything on this one is the container itself dying and being restarted in place.

panels.title: OOMKilled (last termination)
panels.description: Reads 1 while the last termination of that container was an OOM kill. This is a state, not a counter: it stays at 1 until the pod is replaced, and a pod that has never terminated reports nothing at all. Paired with the memory-vs-limit panel it separates the two ways this service dies — killed for exceeding the cgroup limit, versus exiting for any other reason.

panels.title: Pods Up
panels.description: Connectors reach this service over gRPC on GRPC_PORT. A pod that is down is a credential lookup failure for every connector; the gRPC row below is that surface's own RED signals.

panels.title: JWKS Available
panels.description: 1 while the JWT authority key set is loaded, 0 while it is unreachable or empty. Zero does not mean this service is down: the gRPC CredentialService that connectors depend on never touches the JWKS, and this is deliberately kept out of the health probes so Kubernetes does not restart the pod or pull it from the Service over it. What it does mean is that every request to the UI-facing Connect API is being rejected, while the gRPC panels below should be entirely unaffected.

panels.title: Admin API Requests (5m)
panels.description: Requests to the UI-facing Connect API, health and metrics endpoints included.

panels.title: Admin API Errors (5m)
panels.description: Non-2xx responses over the last five minutes.

panels.title: Unauthorized (5m)
panels.description: 401 and 403 together. A sustained climb with JWKS Available at 0 is the signature of a JWT-authority outage rather than a caller problem.

panels.title: In Flight
panels.description: HTTP requests currently being served.

panels.title: JWKS Availability
panels.description: keyfunc does not fail when the JWKS host is unreachable -- it serves an empty key set and retries in the background -- so this gauge is the only signal that the UI-facing API is rejecting everything. Alert on it here: it is deliberately not a health check, because a 503 on /health restarts the pod and an unready pod leaves the Service, cutting off the connector gRPC API over a dependency none of them use.

panels.title: Rejected Requests vs JWKS
panels.description: Overlays the 401/403 rate on the gauge. The two moving together is a JWKS outage; 401s without it are ordinary bad tokens.

panels.title: Request Rate by Method
panels.description: GetConnectorCredential is the hot path: every connector calls it to resolve a datasource credential before it can read anything.

panels.title: Errors by Code
panels.description: code="0" is OK and is excluded. code="5" (NotFound) is a connector asking for a credential that was never provisioned, which is a configuration problem rather than a fault here.

panels.title: Duration p50 / p95 / p99
panels.description: On the SubsecondLatencyBuckets ladder. A connector blocks on this call before it can fetch anything, so latency here is latency for every scan.

panels.title: Error Ratio (non-OK)
panels.description: Share of calls returning a non-OK code.

panels.title: In Flight
panels.description: Concurrent calls being served.

panels.title: Request Rate by Route
panels.description: Per-route throughput. The Connect RPCs share one path prefix.

panels.title: Request Rate by Status
panels.description: 401 and 403 separate out the authentication and authorization failures.

panels.title: Duration p95 by Route
panels.description: Buckets are the SubsecondLatencyBuckets ladder this service opts into, so percentiles are meaningful rather than interpolated inside a single bucket.

panels.title: Error Ratio (non-2xx)
panels.description: Share of responses that are not 2xx.

panels.title: Payload Throughput
panels.description: Request and response bytes. Credential writes carry an opaque Any, so a sudden change in request size is worth a look.

panels.title: In Flight
panels.description: Concurrent requests being served.

panels.title: Request Rate by Pod
panels.description: Uses the .* variable; the aggregate panels above deliberately ignore it.

panels.title: JWKS Availability by Pod
panels.description: A single pod reporting 0 is that replica's keyfunc, not the authority being down.

panels.title: Goroutines
panels.description: Each open SSE stream holds goroutines; a rising floor that never comes back down alongside a flat connection gauge is a leak signal.

panels.title: GC Pause (max)
panels.description: Longest stop-the-world GC pause per pod. go_gc_duration_seconds is a Prometheus summary, not a histogram: there is no _bucket series, so histogram_quantile cannot be used here. The Go collector exposes quantiles 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 and 1 only — there is no 0.99. quantile="1" is the max pause over the runtime's buffer of recent GC cycles, so it reports the worst recent pause rather than a windowed percentile.

panels.title: Open vs Max FDs
panels.description: Long-lived SSE streams each hold a socket, so this is the ceiling that limits concurrent UI subscribers.

panels.title: Process Uptime
panels.description: Time since process start. A restart drops every in-memory SSE session, so sawtooth here explains client reconnect storms.

panels.title: Documents by Outcome (rate)
panels.description:
- This dashboard covers the SIDECAR only: the hub image running as a native sidecar inside `applications-knowledge-service-be-go-*`, reached over loopback. It does every document this platform ingests.
- `succeeded` is the only outcome that wrote a document. `reused` short-circuited on same source_url + same checksum and cost one lock acquisition.
- Read `reused` as saved work, not throughput: leaving it in the same series as `succeeded` would make a redelivery storm look like a capacity increase.
- `cancelled` means the caller disconnected at a checkpoint — knowledge-service giving up, usually its own timeout.

panels.title: Ingest Duration — p50 / p95 / p99
panels.description:
- Admission to terminal outcome, per document.
- Shares a bucket ladder with `knowledge_service_pipeline_ingester_request_duration_seconds` on purpose. Compare them bucket-for-bucket: the GAP is queue and transport, not this service.
- `reused` documents land near zero and pull the p50 down, so read this with the outcome split beside it.

panels.title: Failure Error Codes (rate)
panels.description:
- The classification the caller was handed. Retryability is a property of the class, never of whether the client happened to disconnect.
- `db_unavailable` and `coordination_timeout` are retryable and self-correcting at low rates; a sustained rate means the coordinator pool is the ceiling.
- `malformed_content`, `checksum_mismatch` and `object_too_large` are terminal — retrying those burns the caller's delivery budget for nothing.

panels.title: Reuse & Success Share
panels.description:
- `reused` share rising is redelivery: the same document arriving again with an unchanged checksum. Cheap, but it means work upstream is being repeated.
- `succeeded` share falling while total rate holds is the shape that preceded the 2026-08-26 incident, when the ingester answered `success=false, retryable=false` at 60-550 docs/min and did no real work at all.

panels.title: In Flight vs Queued
panels.description:
- `in_flight` is bounded above by INGEST_MAX_CONCURRENT (10 deployed). `queued` is documents blocked on the admission semaphore.
- In flight pinned at the limit with nothing queued is a busy but healthy sidecar. A rising QUEUE is the point at which raising INGEST_MAX_CONCURRENT — and INGEST_COORDINATOR_POOL_MAX with it — is the remedy rather than more replicas.
- The two never overlap: a document is counted in exactly one of them.

panels.title: Admission Wait p95 by Result
panels.description:
- Waiting is deliberate backpressure, not an error: past the coordinator pool ceiling psycopg raises PoolError, which classifies as a RETRYABLE db_unavailable, so the caller re-sends and adds load to a system already at its limit. Blocking converts that into a queue.
- A `timeout` sample never touched a store — nothing retracted, no ledger row — so it is safe to retry immediately.
- The ladder starts at a 0 bucket so an uncontended admission is distinguishable from one that waited a tenth of a second.

panels.title: Document Lock Wait p95 by Result
panels.description:
- Do NOT read this as capacity. Waiting here means the SAME document is being ingested concurrently — usually a redelivery racing its own original — which is exactly what the per-document coordinator lease exists to serialize.
- Admission and this share ONE budget (INGEST_LOCK_WAIT_SECONDS), so a queued request cannot spend the full budget twice.
- `error` means try_acquire itself raised: pool exhaustion or a lost connection, not contention.

panels.title: Ingest Duration Heatmap
panels.description: - The distribution the percentiles flatten. Two bands usually means two populations — `reused` short-circuits against real ingestions — rather than a bimodal latency problem.

panels.title: Failures by Mutation Phase (rate)
panels.description:
- The metric that says whether a failure was EXPENSIVE.
- `pre_mutation`, `acquire`, `acquire_timeout`, `admission_timeout` touched no store: the prior document is intact and a retry is free.
- `prior_retraction_started` / `new_writes_started` mean prior state was already deleted. The document was retrievable before the attempt and is not now — a retry has to rebuild it.
- `ledger_pending` means the new document is written and READY and only the bookkeeping failed.

panels.title: Rollbacks of Partial Writes (rate)
panels.description:
- Every sample is a document that was mutated and then cleaned up.
- `failed` rising is a dependency problem. `cancelled` rising is callers giving up on us mid-write — check knowledge-service's own timeout before assuming this side is at fault.

panels.title: Ledger Write Failures (rate)
panels.description:
- `op="success"` is the costly one: the document is fully written and READY but the ledger does not say so, so the caller is handed a retryable failure and the WHOLE document is re-ingested to reconcile one row.
- Non-zero here means real work is being redone. It is also invisible everywhere else — the ingestion looks like a failure to the caller and like a success in the stores.

panels.title: Destructive-Phase Failure Share
panels.description: - Share of failures that had already deleted prior state. This is the number to alert on rather than the raw failure rate: a service failing 5% pre-mutation is annoying, a service failing 5% mid-write is losing documents that used to be retrievable.

panels.title: Cached Object Size — p50 / p95
panels.description:
- `stored` is what S3 billed and transferred; `decoded` is what the rest of ingestion actually chews through.
- content-service zstd-compresses the text bucket unconditionally at 10-40x, so without the split the two populations would share one distribution and neither would read.
- A cluster of stored samples against 25 MiB is rejection pressure (INGEST_S3_MAX_OBJECT_BYTES), not a size distribution.

panels.title: Achieved Compression Ratio
panels.description:
- decoded bytes / stored bytes, aggregated. Expect roughly 10-40x on text.
- A ratio collapsing toward 1 means objects are arriving uncompressed — legacy objects with no `codec` metadata key, which is legal but means content-service wrote them by an older path.

panels.title: Cache Read p95 & Error Rate
panels.description:
- Covers the whole read: GET, streaming, checksum compare and zstd decode. Splitting further would need timers around code paths that mostly raise.
- `undecodable_content` at volume is the 2026-08-26 signature: a reader that does not dispatch on the `codec` user-metadata key gets raw zstd bytes and fails every object terminally.

panels.title: Document Bytes Handed to Processing
panels.description:
- `source="cached"` is the V2 path (decoded S3 text); `source="upload"` is a direct upload, which should not occur on the sidecar.
- **Read every stage duration against this.** A slow embedding stage on a 90 MiB document is arithmetic, not a regression.

panels.title: Stage Duration p95
panels.description:
- **Start here when ingestion is slow.** This breakdown exists nowhere else: the caller sees one streaming RPC whose progress frames carry a percentage, not a duration.
- Stages in pipeline order: `parse`, `ontology_infer`, `db_store`, `chunking`, `embedding`, `triple_extraction`, `kg_post`, `finalize`.
- `triple_extraction` normally dominates; descend into the Extraction row below to see whether that is the primary pass or the optional verify/discovery passes, which are the two that can be switched off.

panels.title: Stage Share of Wall Time
panels.description:
- Seconds of work per second, per stage — i.e. how much of the sidecar's concurrent capacity each stage is consuming right now.
- Unlike the p95 next door this is weighted by volume, so a slow stage that runs rarely stays small. It is the panel that answers "what would I optimise", where p95 answers "what is slow".
- The total across stages approximates documents in flight.

panels.title: Processing Duration p95 by Outcome
panels.description:
- DocumentProcessor only, excluding admission, lock and S3 fetch. The gap between this and Ingest Duration on the top row is everything the coordinator does.
- `error` far below `ready` is the healthy shape: failures should be cheap.

panels.title: Records / Chunks / Triples per Document
panels.description:
- What each document actually produced, p50 and p95.
- **A 0-chunk document is not retrievable.** In strict (V2) mode that is a terminal MalformedContentError, so a rise in the p50 sitting at 0 means content is arriving that we cannot chunk.
- Triples at 0 with chunks healthy means extraction found nothing — check the Extraction row rather than assuming failure.

panels.title: Documents In Processing vs Completion Rate
panels.description:
- Stall detection. A flat non-zero in-flight with a completion rate at zero is wedged, not busy — and every histogram goes quiet in that state, so nothing else shows it.
- In-flight is taken inside the per-filename lock, so documents blocked behind a same-filename upload are not counted here.

panels.title: Processing Outcomes (rate)
panels.description:
- `ready` vs `error` leaving DocumentProcessor. Counts documents, not attempts.
- Compare with Documents by Outcome at the top: a document can process to READY and still fail the ingestion at the ledger step.

panels.title: Vector Operation p95

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, operation, status) (rate(knowledge_hub_vector_operation_duration_seconds_bucket{job=~".*knowledge-hub-be-go-sidecar", namespace="default"}[5m])))

panels.description:
- `add_chunks` is the whole embed-and-write stage; `upsert` / `put_vectors` is the write alone, instrumented separately because the Pinecone and S3 Vectors stores LOG AND SWALLOW their write failures.
- That is why `status="error"` on the write operation matters more than it looks: `add_chunks` returns normally in that case and reports success.

panels.title: Chunks Written vs Chunks Produced
panels.description:
- **The silent-data-loss check.** `produced` is what chunking made; `written` is what the vector store acknowledged.
- These should track each other exactly. A persistent gap means writes are being dropped by the swallow described next door, and the documents involved are indexed as READY while being unsearchable.

panels.title: Embedding Batches (rate)
panels.description:
- The embedding stage is one long call from the outside. This is the only evidence a large document is ADVANCING through it rather than hanging.
- A flat rate with `embedding` rising on the stage p95 is a stalled embedding provider.

panels.title: Graph & Database Write p95
panels.description:
- Triple writes and the per-document record store. `add_triples` on Neptune fans out into many round trips; see the Neptune panel on the standalone Overview for the per-request view.
- `store_document` slow with a healthy `query` usually means the shared PostgreSQL is write-saturated by concurrent sidecars, not that this document is unusual.

panels.title: Extraction Phase p95
panels.description:
- The breakdown behind `stage="triple_extraction"`, which is usually the dominant stage.
- `pass1` is the primary guided/dynamic extraction. `pass2` (discovery), `verify` and `tabular` are optional passes — if they dominate, they are the levers.

panels.title: Model Calls by Status (rate)
panels.description:
- Extraction fires many short prompts per document, so this rate is roughly records-per-second, not documents-per-second.
- `error` includes a throttle that exhausted botocore's adaptive retries; a rise here with rising stage p95 is Bedrock quota, not model latency.

panels.title: Tokens per Second
panels.description: - Ingestion token spend. Multiply by the per-model rate for cost; the model label is what makes that computable from the series alone.

panels.title: Prompt Cache Hit Ratio
panels.description:
- Process-local cache keyed by sha256(model_id + prompt), 2048 entries, FIFO.
- Expected to be LOW: the same record rarely repeats within one ingestion. A high ratio means the corpus is repetitive; a ratio near zero is normal and not a fault.
- Note the cache is per pod, so it resets on every sidecar restart.

panels.title: Container Memory (working set) per Pod
panels.description:
- This dashboard covers the SIDECAR: the hub image running inside `applications-knowledge-service-be-go-*` as an initContainer with `restartPolicy: Always`. Container series are selected by pod name + `container="knowledge-hub-be-go"` because cAdvisor metrics carry no `job` label.
- **This is what the kubelet counts against the 1Gi limit and what triggers an OOM kill.**
- Open issue: every incarnation since ~2026-08-26 starts near 150-200 MiB and climbs monotonically for as long as it lives (peak observed 368.8 MiB). No incarnation has lived long enough to show a plateau — they are all cut short by deploys — so leak vs working set is still undecided.
- Watch ONE incarnation. The growth is invisible across pod restarts, which is exactly why it went unnoticed.

panels.title: Growth Rate (MiB/min)
panels.description:
- `deriv` over the trailing hour. The measured figure during the open investigation was **+1.125 MiB/min** for this container against +0.019 for the knowledge-service worker beside it.
- Sustained positive with a flat document rate is the leak shape. Positive only while throughput rises is a working set.
- Needs an hour of one incarnation to mean anything; it reads as noise right after a deploy.

panels.title: Retained Bytes per Completed Upload

targets.expr: sum by (pod) (deriv(process_resident_memory_bytes{job=~".*knowledge-hub-be-go-sidecar", namespace="default", pod=~".*"}[1h])) / clamp_min(sum by (pod) (rate(knowledge_hub_ingest_documents_total{job=~".*knowledge-hub-be-go-sidecar", namespace="default", outcome="succeeded", pod=~".*"}[1h])), 0.0001)

panels.description:
- Memory growth divided by the rate of `outcome="succeeded"` ingestions: **how much this process keeps for every document it finishes.**
- Crude arithmetic during the investigation put it at ~63 KiB per completed upload. That number sizes the search; it is not a claim about where it goes.
- This is the panel that decides the question. A figure that FALLS as throughput rises is a working set. A flat, non-zero figure is a per-document leak.
- Meaningless when the success rate is near zero — the denominator collapses. Read it against the Ingestion dashboard's outcome panel.

panels.title: Process Resident Memory vs Working Set
panels.description:
- RSS is what the Python process holds; working set is what the kubelet bills. They should track; a widening gap is page cache, not the interpreter.
- RSS is newly available for this container — before the metrics endpoint was exposed on the sidecar port there was no `process_*` or `python_*` series for it at all, and the cgroup number was the only thing graphable.

panels.title: Memory by Container

targets.expr: sum by (pod, container) (container_memory_working_set_bytes{namespace="default", pod=~".*knowledge-service-be-go.*", container!="", container!="POD"})

panels.description:
- Both containers in the knowledge-service pod. The sidecar has been ~92% of the pod total, which is what made a hub memory climb read as a knowledge-service leak.
- Limits are PER CONTAINER — knowledge-service 512Mi, the hub sidecar 1Gi — so a summed pod figure compares against neither.

panels.title: CPU by Container

targets.expr: sum by (pod, container) (rate(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total{namespace="default", pod=~".*knowledge-service-be-go.*", container!="", container!="POD"}[5m]))

panels.description:
- Cores. The hub sidecar is the CPU-heavy one: parsing, chunking and embedding are all synchronous Python on executor threads.
- Throttling shows up as stage durations rising with no change in document size — cross-check the Ingestion dashboard's stage panel.

panels.title: Restarts by Container (1h increase)
panels.description:
- Zero over 24h for this container throughout the memory investigation, which is the main evidence the growth has not yet reached an OOM.
- A sidecar restart breaks in-flight uploads: expect INGESTER_UPLOAD_FAILED retries on knowledge-service rather than abandoned batches.
- Because it is a native sidecar, the worker does not start until this container has Started and is not terminated until the worker exits.

panels.title: Incarnation Age
panels.description:
- Time since this process started. **Read every memory panel against it**: the growth is only visible within a single incarnation, and every incarnation so far has been replaced by a deploy inside about two hours.
- Deciding leak vs working set needs one of these to run for several hours under load.

panels.title: GC Pause p95 by Generation
panels.description:
- Ingestion allocates heavily and in bursts — parsed record structures, chunk lists, triple objects — and a gen-2 collection over that heap stalls the event loop exactly like a blocking call, but attributed to nothing.
- Read with Event Loop Lag below: lag WITH matching gen-2 pauses is memory pressure; lag WITHOUT them is blocking code on the loop.

panels.title: GC Collections (rate)
panels.description:
- Collections per second per generation, from the standard `python_gc_collections_total` collector.
- A rising gen-2 rate alongside rising memory means the collector is running and NOT reclaiming — the strongest available hint that something holds references rather than that allocation simply increased.

panels.title: Objects Collected (rate)
panels.description: - Objects reclaimed per second. Compare with the collection rate: many collections reclaiming few objects is the signature of a growing live set.

panels.title: Uncollectable Objects (rate)
panels.description: - Objects the collector could not free. Should be zero. Non-zero means reference cycles involving objects it cannot reclaim, which would be a direct explanation for the growth.

panels.title: Event Loop Lag — p95 / p99
panels.description:
- One asyncio loop serves every upload stream on this sidecar while ingestion runs synchronously on executor threads. Anything CPU-bound that lands ON the loop delays every in-flight upload at once.
- No individual operation looks slow when this happens: the work still completes, just after the loop is handed back. This is the only series that shows it.
- A scrape of `/metrics` queues behind the loop too, so sustained lag also shows up as scrape timeouts.

panels.title: OS Threads
panels.description:
- Each streaming ingestion RPC builds its own single-worker ThreadPoolExecutor, so this rises and falls with concurrent uploads.
- **A monotonic climb that survives idle periods is an executor that is not being shut down** — and would be a candidate explanation for the memory growth, since each thread carries a stack.

panels.title: Asyncio Tasks
panels.description:
- Tasks alive on the loop, which is the streaming layer's own queue depth: RPCs in flight plus the progress-drain machinery behind them.
- Should track ingestions in flight. Growing without them is leaked tasks.

panels.title: Ingest Slots — In Flight vs Queued
panels.description:
- Repeated from the Ingestion dashboard because memory is expected to scale with CONCURRENT documents, not with cumulative ones.
- Memory rising while this stays flat is the observation that makes a working-set explanation hard to sustain.

panels.title: Process CPU (rate)
panels.description: - Cores consumed by the hub process itself, as opposed to the cgroup figure above.

panels.title: Open vs Max File Descriptors
panels.description: - Each in-flight upload holds an S3 connection and a coordinator connection. A climb tracking uptime rather than concurrency is a descriptor leak.

panels.title: Ingestion Throughput (context)
panels.description: - Present so every memory panel above can be read against load. The regime change in the open investigation coincided with the SUCCESS path starting to run at volume — request volume actually FELL across the transition.

panels.title: Cumulative Documents This Incarnation
panels.description:
- Documents completed since this process started. The investigation's per-upload arithmetic used ~1,870 completed uploads against +115 MiB.
- Plot against working set: a straight line through the origin is a per-document leak, a curve that flattens is a working set reaching steady state.

panels.title: Pods Up
panels.description:
- This dashboard covers the STANDALONE deployment only: `applications-knowledge-hub-be-go-*`, the pod serving the Connect API behind Kong.
- The selector `job=~".*knowledge-hub-be-go"` has no trailing `.*`, and Prometheus matchers are fully anchored, so it deliberately EXCLUDES `...-knowledge-hub-be-go-sidecar`.
- The same image also runs as an ingestor sidecar inside the knowledge-service pod. That instance does completely different work and has its own two dashboards.

panels.title: RPC Rate
panels.description: All Connect procedures across the four mounted services.

panels.title: RPC p95
panels.description: All procedures pooled. Split by procedure below — a chat stream and a metadata list do not belong in one number.

panels.title: RPC Error Ratio
panels.description:
- Share of calls ending in a Connect code other than `ok`.
- This is the WIRE outcome. A document that failed to ingest but whose stream completed cleanly is `ok` here; that verdict lives on the ingestion dashboard.

panels.title: Request Rate by Procedure
panels.description:
- One series per fully qualified `service/method`.
- The label set is closed — it comes from the generated method descriptor — so it cannot grow with traffic.

panels.title: p95 by Procedure
panels.description:
- Where user-facing latency actually is. Chat synthesis and knowledge-graph traversal dominate; metadata reads should be milliseconds.
- Buckets run 5ms to 1800s, so a chat stream held open for minutes is still resolvable rather than piling into `+Inf`.

panels.title: Connect Codes (rate)
panels.description:
- `ok` is excluded so a low error rate is still legible.
- `unauthenticated` / `permission_denied` are the auth interceptor. `invalid_argument` is usually a client schema mistake, reclassified from a protobuf decode error by ProtoDecodeErrorMiddleware.
- `unknown` is the one to chase: it means an exception escaped a handler.

panels.title: In Flight by Procedure
panels.description:
- Calls currently executing. This is what separates STALLED from IDLE: a wedged dependency observes no durations at all, so the histograms go quiet and the two look identical.
- A procedure pinned above zero with no completions is the shape to alert on.

panels.title: Vector Search p95

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, backend) (rate(knowledge_hub_vector_operation_duration_seconds_bucket{job=~".*knowledge-hub-be-go", namespace="default", operation="search"}[5m])))

panels.description:
- `operation="search"` only: the read path behind chat and document search. Writes happen on the sidecar, not here.
- `backend` is whichever of chromadb / pinecone / s3vectors this deployment resolved to at startup.

panels.title: Graph Operation p95
panels.description:
- Knowledge-graph reads serving entity context and citation grounding.
- On Neptune, read against Neptune Round Trip next door: a slow operation with fast round trips means we are making too many of them, which is a query-shape problem rather than a Neptune one.

panels.title: Neptune Round Trip p95 & Retries
panels.description:
- One signed openCypher HTTP round trip, timed including retries and backoff sleeps because that is what the caller waits for.
- Retries are counted separately: one slow response and three fast failures with two backoffs are indistinguishable on the duration alone.
- Absent entirely when GRAPH_STORE_BACKEND is the local NetworkX store.

panels.title: Document Database p95 by Operation
panels.description:
- `query` is the SQL-expert path answering analytical questions; `get_schema` feeds the prompt that writes those queries.
- `store_document` should sit near zero here — ingestion runs on the sidecar.

panels.title: Model Call Rate by Status
panels.description:
- Chat synthesis, entity canonicalization and the agent tools all land here.
- `error` counts a call that raised, including a throttle that exhausted botocore's adaptive retries.

panels.title: Model Call p95 by Model
panels.description:
- Three model ids at most: the default (Maverick), the fast one (Scout), and the synthesis model (Claude Sonnet), which is pinned in code rather than by env var.
- Synthesis is one call per query on the critical final answer, so its p95 is most of the user's wait.

panels.title: Tokens per Second
panels.description:
- The cost metric: spend is tokens x per-model rate, and the model label is what makes that computable from the series alone.
- Output tokens bill several times higher than input on every model here, so watch the two separately.

panels.title: Tokens per Call
panels.description:
- Mean tokens per invocation — prompt size rather than volume.
- A step change here with a flat call rate means the prompt got bigger, usually more retrieved context rather than more traffic.

panels.title: Ingest Outcomes (rate)
panels.description:
- **This should be flat at zero.** knowledge-service dials the ingestor sidecar over loopback, so no document should reach the standalone pod.
- Non-zero means something is calling `content.v1.ContentService` through the Service or Kong. Worth knowing: this pod shares no admission budget with the sidecars, and INGEST_MAX_CONCURRENT was sized against the coordinator pool on the assumption it is idle.
- If it is legitimately non-zero, the sidecar Ingestion dashboard's panels all work against this job too — change the selector.

panels.title: Documents In Processing
panels.description: - DocumentProcessor concurrency on this pod. Same expectation as the panel beside it: flat at zero.

panels.title: Event Loop Lag p95 / p99
panels.description:
- One asyncio loop serves every RPC on this pod, so anything CPU-bound that runs ON the loop delays every in-flight call at once — and no individual operation looks slow when it does.
- Sustained lag alongside healthy dependency latencies means blocking code, not a slow backend. Check GC pauses on the Runtime dashboard before concluding either.

panels.title: Resident Memory by Pod
panels.description:
- On the overview because it is half of an open question: the sidecar instance of this same image grows monotonically under real ingest while this one has sat flat (149.4 MiB over an 80-minute window, unchanged to one decimal).
- A climb HERE would break that asymmetry and would be the strongest available clue about the cause. Full breakdown on the Runtime dashboard.

panels.title: Process CPU (rate)
panels.description:
- This dashboard covers the STANDALONE deployment only. Container series are selected on `pod=~".*knowledge-hub-be-go-.*"`, which does not match `...-knowledge-service-be-go-...` and therefore excludes the sidecar copy of this image.
- Cores consumed serving the Connect API. This pod does not ingest, so CPU should track query volume and chat synthesis, not document size.

panels.title: Process Resident Memory
panels.description:
- Physical memory held by the process, per pod.
- Measured flat at 149.4 MiB across an 80-minute window during the sidecar memory investigation — unchanged to one decimal place while the sidecar copy of the same image climbed steadily.
- **A climb here would be significant**: it would mean the growth is not specific to the upload path, which is currently the leading hypothesis.

panels.title: Container Memory (working set)
panels.description:
- What the kubelet counts against the limit and what triggers an OOM kill. This, not resident memory, is the number to compare against a limit.
- The standalone Deployment sets no memory limit today; the sidecar copy is capped at 1Gi.

panels.title: GC Pause p95 by Generation
panels.description:
- Stop-the-world collection time. On this pod the heap is dominated by cached query results and ontology cards rather than by document structures, so gen-2 pauses should be short and rare.
- Read with Event Loop Lag: lag with matching gen-2 pauses is memory pressure; lag without them is blocking code on the loop.

panels.title: GC Collections (rate)
panels.description: - From the standard `python_gc_collections_total` collector, registered for free by prometheus_client.

panels.title: Objects Collected (rate)
panels.description: - Objects reclaimed per second. Many collections reclaiming few objects is the signature of a growing live set.

panels.title: Uncollectable Objects (rate)
panels.description: - Should be zero. Non-zero means reference cycles the collector cannot free.

panels.title: Event Loop Lag — p95 / p99
panels.description:
- One asyncio loop serves every RPC on this pod, including the chat stream. Anything CPU-bound that runs ON the loop delays every in-flight call at once, and no individual operation looks slow when it happens.
- This pod is more exposed to it than the sidecar: its callers are people waiting on a UI, not a retrying worker.

panels.title: OS Threads
panels.description:
- Each streaming RPC builds its own single-worker ThreadPoolExecutor, so this rises and falls with concurrent streams.
- A monotonic climb surviving idle periods is an executor that is not being shut down.

panels.title: Asyncio Tasks
panels.description: - Tasks alive on the loop. Should track RPCs in flight; growing without them is leaked tasks.

panels.title: RPCs In Flight
panels.description: - Present here so the two panels beside it can be read against real concurrency rather than against uptime.

panels.title: Open vs Max File Descriptors
panels.description: - Connections to PostgreSQL, the vector store, Neptune and Bedrock all consume descriptors. A climb tracking uptime rather than concurrency is a leak.

panels.title: Process Uptime
panels.description: - Time since the process started. A reset without a deploy means a crash or an OOM kill — cross-check restarts.

panels.title: Container Restarts (1h increase)
panels.description:
- Any non-zero outside a deploy needs a reason: OOM kill, probe failure, or an import-time configuration failure.
- The last of those is worth knowing about: `build_app` validates deployment config at import, so a misconfigured pod exits non-zero at startup rather than serving traffic in a degraded state.

panels.title: Container CPU Usage
panels.description: - The cgroup figure, as opposed to the process figure at the top. A gap between them means other processes in the container.

panels.title: Pods Up
panels.description:
- Scrape targets reporting `up` for this service in the namespace.
- Should equal the replica count. Below it means pods are crashlooping or not being scraped.
- Zero while JE_KNOWLEDGE has a backlog means nothing is consuming the stream.

panels.title: Documents In Flight
panels.description:
- Documents inside a worker right now, summed over pods. Ceiling is WORKER_POOL_SIZE x pods.
- Non-zero with zero throughput means work is stuck, not idle — that distinction is the whole reason this gauge exists.
- Zero with a JetStream backlog means handlers are not picking work up at all.

panels.title: Ingested (rate)
panels.description:
- `outcome="forwarded"` only — the single outcome meaning the ingester actually accepted the document.
- This is the real progress number. Every other outcome is forwarded too, but was not ingested.
- Read against Not Ingested: these two being the same order of magnitude is a problem.

panels.title: Not Ingested (rate)
panels.description:
- `outcome!="forwarded"` — every document that reached a terminal outcome without being ingested.
- Two different failures land here: `forwarded_not_ingested` is the ingester's own verdict (see Ingest Failure Ratio); `failed_permanent` is this service giving up (see Permanent Failures by Error Code).
- NOT a loss rate — the item is still forwarded downstream carrying its failure in `knowledge_hub`.
- Retryable conditions never reach here; they are retried in-process until they resolve.
- The negative matcher is deliberate: the outcome set is open, so a new terminal value is counted the day it ships rather than going silently missing.

panels.title: Processing p95
panels.description:
- 95th percentile of one document's life: first submission to terminal outcome, spanning every in-process retry pass.
- Buckets run 0.1s to 3600s. A p95 sitting at the top bucket means stuck, not slow — go to the Pipeline dashboard's Convergence panel.
- Rising while the ingested rate stays flat means documents are waiting on a dependency rather than working.

panels.title: Ingest Failure Ratio
panels.description:
- `forwarded_not_ingested` as a share of everything forwarded.
- The ingester accepted the call and reported success == false, so the item still moves downstream carrying the failure.
- An ingest-failure rate, not a pipeline-failure rate — the fix is in the ingester or the source content, not here.
- No clamp on the denominator: with no traffic this returns no data rather than a misleading 0%.

panels.title: Outcomes by Type (rate)
panels.description:
- `forwarded` = ingested. `forwarded_not_ingested` = the ingester's terminal no. `failed_permanent` = this service gave up.
- One sample per document, not per attempt — retries are in-process and counted on `document_retries_total`.
- All three are forwarded downstream. They differ in whether the document was ingested, not in whether it survived.
- The three together are the true document completion rate; compare it against intake on the Pipeline dashboard.

panels.title: Permanent Failures by Error Code
panels.description:
- `outcome="failed_permanent"` only, split by the code written into `knowledge_hub.msg`.
- These are not ItemErrors — the code rides downstream on the document itself.
- `EXTRACTION_ERROR` / `CONTENT_ERROR` are content-service's terminal verdict. `INGESTER_REJECTED` / `INVALID_INGEST_REQUEST` mean the ingester refused the request shape, which is our bug rather than the document's.
- A new code appearing is worth chasing. A shifting mix among existing ones usually just means the corpus changed.

panels.title: Ingest vs Retry vs Not Ingested (rate)
panels.description:
- `ingested` — real progress (`outcome="forwarded"`).
- `retrying (per pass)` — in-process churn from `document_retries_total`. Counted per pass, so it can exceed the document rate. Not loss, and never sum it with the others.
- `rejected by ingester` — the ingester's own terminal verdict (`forwarded_not_ingested`).
- `gave up (this service)` — `failed_permanent`.
- ingested + rejected + gave up covers every terminal outcome, so those three sum to the document rate. Nothing here is a dropped document.
- Retries climbing while ingested stays flat is the stall signature — go to Convergence on the Pipeline dashboard.

panels.title: Processing Duration — p50 / p95 / p99
panels.description:
- One document, first submission to terminal outcome, across every retry pass it took.
- p50 is the common path; p99 is documents waiting on a dependency.
- p50 flat with p99 climbing means a slow minority, usually content extraction. All three climbing means a dependency is slow for everything.
- Buckets end at 3600s — anything pinned at the top bucket is stuck, not slow.

panels.title: Processing p95 by Outcome
panels.description:
- The same measure split by outcome, because outcomes fail at different speeds.
- `failed_permanent` usually fails fast, so mixing it in drags the `forwarded` quantile down and hides a real slowdown.
- Watch `forwarded` alone as the latency SLI.

panels.title: Dependency p95 (success path)
panels.description:
- `content` is our GetContent call; `ingester` is our streaming upload.
- `status="success"` only, so fast failures do not land in the same bucket stream as real work.
- content approaching CONTENT_GET_TIMEOUT (120s) means we are timing out and re-asking rather than getting answers.
- ingester climbing toward INGESTER_UPLOAD_TIMEOUT (600s) means uploads are the bottleneck — check Worker Pool on the Pipeline dashboard.

panels.title: Dependency Requests In Flight
panels.description:
- Concurrent outbound calls per dependency, service-wide.
- Localizes a stall: sustained non-zero here with flat throughput points at the named dependency rather than at this service.
- The ceiling is WORKER_POOL_SIZE — pinned there means every worker is blocked inside that one dependency.

panels.title: Dependency Error Rate
panels.description:
- Derived from each duration histogram's `_count` with `status="error"`: transport failures plus responses carrying an application error instead of usable data.
- A content spike with a flat ingester line points at content-service or NATS; both rising together is usually the network or this pod.
- Errors here are not losses — each becomes a retry or a failure recorded on the document.

panels.title: Batches Received by Kind (rate)
panels.description:
- `multi` and `single` are both upstream batches and differ only in size; `empty` is ACKed without work.
- A batch is the unit of work and is processed to completion in place — this service does not fan out.
- Every non-empty batch should eventually be matched by a forwarded one.
- Batch size is chosen by the producer (the extractor), not here — see the pipeline step's `config`.

panels.title: Batches Forwarded vs Received (rate)
panels.description:
- `received (non-empty)` — batches taken off JetStream.
- `forwarded success` — every document in the batch reached a terminal outcome and the batch was published on.
- `forwarded error` — PublishToNext failed, which fails the whole batch and returns it to JobEngine for redelivery.
- Forwarded lagging received is the normal shape while batches are in flight. A persistent, widening gap means batches are being held — check Retry Queue Depth and Worker Pool.

panels.title: Batch Duration — p50 / p95 / p99
panels.description:
- Receipt to forwarding, per batch. Buckets 1s to 8192s (~2.3h).
- Gated by the slowest document in the batch, because nothing is forwarded until everything is terminal — so this tracks the tail of document latency, not its middle.
- Large batches make this worse mechanically: halving the producer's batch size roughly halves this without changing per-document latency.

panels.title: Batches Abandoned on Shutdown (rate)
panels.description:
- The pod was shutting down with documents still retryable, so the ItemBatch goes back to JetStream for another pod.
- Nothing is lost — content-service serves the redone work from cache and the ingester dedupes on content_sha256.
- Expect a burst on every deploy. A steady non-zero rate OUTSIDE a deploy is the real signal: batches routinely outlive the pods running them, so either documents are slower than the pod lifetime or pods are being cycled too aggressively.
- This is the term that makes the counts reconcile: received = forwarded(success) + forwarded(error) + abandoned + still in flight.

panels.title: Retry Queue Depth by Phase
panels.description:
- Documents waiting on a retry, summed across every batch in flight on every pod.
- THE LIVENESS SIGNAL FOR AN UNBOUNDED LOOP: the retry loop has no attempt cap and no deadline by design, so depth returning to zero is the only evidence that batches converge.
- A floor that never reaches zero means at least one document is stuck and is holding its whole batch open.
- The phase names which dependency to go and look at.

panels.title: Retry Passes by Phase (rate)
panels.description:
- `content` — content-service has not finished with the document, or our own call timed out, which usually means the same thing.
- `knowledge_processing` — content resolved and the ingester has not finished. These resume at the ingester and do not re-resolve content.
- A high content rate with normal completions is ordinary cache-warming on slow extractions.
- A high rate with no completions is not — go to Convergence below.

panels.title: Convergence — Retries vs Completions
panels.description:
- `retries/s` — retry passes. `completions/s` — documents reaching a terminal outcome. `queued for retry` — current depth.
- The non-convergence detector, and the first panel to look at when a scan seems stalled.
- Retries rising while completions stay flat means the loop is spinning on documents it will never finish. Nothing is dropped — that is the design — but nothing progresses either, and every affected batch holds its JetStream message and its workers.
- Healthy shape: retries and completions move together and depth oscillates back to zero.

panels.title: Batch Iterations — p50 / p95
panels.description:
- Retry passes performed per batch. A batch whose documents all succeed first time records 0. Buckets are 0, then 1 to 512.
- Rising p95 with stable batch duration means many cheap passes; rising together means slow ones.
- Observed only when a batch finishes, so no data while batches are being received means no batch has completed yet.

panels.title: Content Rounds per Batch — p50 / p95
panels.description:
- Passes per batch that made content-service calls. The seed pass asks content about every item, so the minimum is 1, never 0.
- Counted per pass, not per call: one round means "this pass asked content about at least one document", however many that was.
- Read against Batch Iterations above. Equal values mean the batch went back to content on every pass — a cold corpus where cache-warming is not converging. Iterations well above rounds mean content resolved early and the extra passes belong to the ingester.
- Rising here alongside CONTENT_TIMEOUT on Retry Reasons is the cache-warming loop working; what it needs is time, not configuration.
- Observed only when a batch finishes, so no data while batches are being received means no batch has completed yet.

panels.title: Retry Reasons by Phase and Error Code (rate)
panels.description:
- Why the loop is turning. The phase alone does not say — the content phase retries on four codes calling for four different responses.
- `CONTENT_TIMEOUT` — content-service did not answer inside our window; usually a slow extraction and ordinary cache-warming.
- `GET_CONTENT_FAILED` — the NATS path itself, so a spike is transport, not documents.
- `CONTENT_ERROR_RETRYABLE` / `EXTRACTION_ERROR_RETRYABLE` — content-service reporting on the document and not having given up on it.
- `INGESTER_UPLOAD_FAILED` / `INGEST_UNSUCCESSFUL_RETRYABLE` — the ingester; these resume at the ingester without re-resolving content.
- An EMPTY error_code is not a dependency failure at all: the worker pool refused the submission, which only happens while the pod is draining. Expect it alongside Batches Abandoned and nowhere else.

panels.title: Documents by Outcome (rate)
panels.description:
- `forwarded` = ingested. `forwarded_not_ingested` = the ingester's own terminal verdict. `failed_permanent` = this service giving up.
- One sample per document, not per attempt — retries are counted on `document_retries_total` — so this is a true document rate.
- The document is forwarded in all three cases, carrying its failure in `knowledge_hub`, so none of them is a loss.
- Compare the sum against intake above to see whether documents are finishing as fast as they arrive.

panels.title: Error Codes by Outcome (rate)
panels.description:
- The failure recorded on each document, which is also what downstream reads out of `knowledge_hub.msg`.
- The empty code is filtered out here; it is the normal case for a clean success.
- These are NOT ItemErrors — every code here rides downstream on the document instead.
- The outcome/code pairing is what carries the meaning: the same code under an unexpected outcome is worth chasing.

panels.title: Unrecorded Failures (rate)
panels.description:
- SHOULD SIT AT ZERO.
- Documents whose verdict could not be written onto the document itself because the payload could not be unmarshalled or re-marshalled — the carrier is the thing that is broken — so they were published as ItemErrors instead.
- The only path in this service that still writes to the job's item-errors hash.
- Anything above zero means malformed payloads are arriving from upstream. Fix the producer; there is nothing to tune here.

panels.title: Document Duration Heatmap
panels.description:
- Per document, first submission to terminal outcome, spanning every retry pass rather than only the last. Buckets 0.1s to 3600s.
- Colour is documents per second landing in each band.
- A bimodal picture is normal: cache hits low, first-time extractions higher.
- Weight collecting in the top band means documents are looping, not working — cross-check Convergence.

panels.title: Document Duration — p50 / p95 / p99
panels.description:
- The same measure as the heatmap above, as quantiles.
- p50 is the common path; p99 is documents waiting on a dependency.
- p50 and p99 diverging means a slow minority. All three rising means a dependency is slow for everything.
- Batch Duration is gated by the worst document here, so the two panels should move together.

panels.title: Document p95 by Outcome
panels.description:
- Split by outcome because outcomes fail at different speeds.
- `failed_permanent` usually fails fast and drags a combined quantile down, so `forwarded` alone is the number to watch.
- `forwarded_not_ingested` slower than `forwarded` means the ingester is doing real work before saying no.

panels.title: Content GetContent — p50 / p95 / p99 (success)
panels.description:
- `status` is success only when the call returned a usable cache location. A transport failure, an application error and a missing cache location are all error.
- This measures OUR call, not content-service's work: our per-call timeout sits below its extraction budget.
- So a slow document appears here as a timed-out error call and then as a fast success on a later retry once the result is cached.
- p95 approaching CONTENT_GET_TIMEOUT (120s) means we are re-asking rather than getting answers — check Retry Reasons for CONTENT_TIMEOUT.

panels.title: Ingester Upload — p50 / p95 / p99 (success)
panels.description:
- `status` here reflects only whether the streaming call completed.
- A terminal frame reporting success == false is still a success on this histogram — that result is carried by the `forwarded_not_ingested` outcome instead.
- Buckets run to 900s, above INGESTER_UPLOAD_TIMEOUT (600s), so a timeout is separable from a slow upload.
- This is usually the dominant term in document duration: if p50 is tens of seconds, the worker pool will saturate.

panels.title: Dependency Call Rate by Status
panels.description:
- Call volume from each histogram's `_count`, split by dependency and status.
- Content calls exceed document count whenever documents are retrying; ingester calls do the same on the knowledge phase.
- A rising error share on one dependency with the other flat localizes the fault.
- Content success count against the document rate shows how much of the work is repeat asking rather than progress.

panels.title: Ingester Stream — Progress Frames vs In Flight
panels.description:
- `progress frames/s` — mid-upload frames received. `ingester in flight` — concurrent uploads.
- The service's own stall signal, and the reason progress frames are counted at all: the frames are otherwise discarded.
- A flat frame rate together with a non-zero in-flight count is a stalled upload stream.
- Either one alone is normal — no in-flight means idle, and frames without in-flight cannot happen.

panels.title: Documents In Flight vs Completion Rate
panels.description:
- `documents in flight` — documents inside a worker right now. `completions/s` — documents reaching a terminal outcome. `{{dependency}} in flight` — which dependency they are sitting in.
- In flight with no completions and no retries is genuinely stuck inside a dependency call, and the dependency line names which one.
- In flight with retries climbing is the loop working — that case belongs to Convergence above.
- Both at zero is idle.

panels.title: Worker Pool — Queued vs Executing
panels.description:
- One pool per pod, shared by every batch that pod is handling. Both series are pod-wide, not per batch.
- `executing` — documents a worker is running right now. Hard ceiling: WORKER_POOL_SIZE.
- `queued` — documents submitted but not yet started. Ceiling: WORKER_QUEUE_DEPTH, plus one more for each handler blocked trying to submit (up to NATS_WORKERS).
- A document is counted in both for an instant during handoff and never in neither, so the sum is the honest submitted-and-unfinished figure and should never dip.
- `executing` pinned at WORKER_POOL_SIZE with little queued: the DEPENDENCIES are slow. A bigger pool would only add pressure to them.
- Sustained queueing while executing sits below its ceiling: the POOL is the bottleneck. WORKER_POOL_SIZE is what to raise.
- `queued` pinned at WORKER_QUEUE_DEPTH + NATS_WORKERS: every handler is blocked in Submit. A batch submits all of its documents before collecting any result, so in this state no batch reaches its accounting stage — terminal-outcome, retry and forward metrics stop appearing across both dashboards even though uploads are still completing. Reduce the producer's batch size or raise the queue.

panels.title: Process CPU (rate)
panels.description:
- CPU seconds per second per pod. 1.0 is one full core.
- This service is I/O-bound — it waits on content-service and the ingester — so CPU should stay low even with the pool full.
- High CPU with low throughput points at marshalling or logging cost, not document work.

panels.title: Process Resident Memory
panels.description:
- Physical memory held by the process, per pod.
- Should track batch size times document size, not uptime. A monotonic climb across batches is a leak.
- The container limit is enforced against working set, not this — see Container Memory below.

panels.title: Process Virtual Memory
panels.description:
- Address space reserved per pod, most of it never resident.
- Go reserves large arenas, so a big number here is normal and not a problem on its own.
- Useful only to confirm that a resident-memory climb is real allocation rather than reservation.

panels.title: Container CPU Usage
panels.description:
- The same work as Process CPU but measured by the kubelet, and split per container.
- One series per container in the pod, including sidecars. `knowledge-service-be-go` is the series that corresponds to the Process CPU panel; everything else is a co-tenant.
- The CPU limit is per container, not per pod — compare each series against its own container's limit.
- Approaching a limit causes throttling, which surfaces as latency everywhere else rather than as an error.

targets.expr: sum by (pod, container) (rate(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total{namespace="default", pod=~".*knowledge-service-be-go.*", container!="", container!="POD"}[5m]))

panels.title: Container Memory (working set)
panels.description:
- What the kubelet counts against the memory limit, and what triggers an OOM kill. This, not resident memory, is the number to compare against a limit.
- One series per container in the pod, including sidecars. `knowledge-hub-be-go` runs here as a native sidecar (the ingester on 127.0.0.1:8080) and normally uses an order of magnitude more memory than the service itself.
- Limits are per container: knowledge-service 512Mi, the knowledge-hub sidecar 1Gi. A summed figure compares against neither.
- A step up that never comes back down after a large batch is the shape to watch — on whichever series shows it.
- An OOM kill shows up as a restart on the panel below, not as a spike here.

targets.expr: sum by (pod, container) (container_memory_working_set_bytes{namespace="default", pod=~".*knowledge-service-be-go.*", container!="", container!="POD"})

panels.title: Goroutines
panels.description:
- Concurrency is bounded by the worker pool, not by document count: expect roughly WORKER_POOL_SIZE plus the JobEngine handlers plus NATS and runtime goroutines.
- Should be flat and boring. A climb that does not come back down alongside a flat documents_in_flight is a leak, not load.
- A step change at a deploy is a config change (pool size, NATS workers), not a leak.

panels.title: Heap In-Use
panels.description:
- Bytes in in-use heap spans, per pod. A sawtooth between GC cycles is normal.
- The FLOOR of the sawtooth is the real working set — a rising floor is the leak signal, not the peaks.
- Correlate a rising floor with Goroutines to tell a goroutine leak from a data leak.

panels.title: GC Pause (max)
panels.description:
- Longest stop-the-world GC pause per pod.
- `go_gc_duration_seconds` is a Prometheus summary, not a histogram: there is no `_bucket` series, so `histogram_quantile` cannot be used here. The Go collector exposes quantiles 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 and 1 only — there is no 0.99.
- `quantile="1"` is the max pause over the runtime's buffer of recent GC cycles, so it reports the worst recent pause rather than a windowed percentile.
- Milliseconds are normal. This is not what makes this service slow — look at the dependency panels first.

panels.title: Open vs Max FDs
panels.description:
- `open` is descriptors held; `max` is the process limit.
- Each NATS connection, gRPC connection and upload stream costs descriptors.
- `open` climbing toward `max` means connections are not being closed; hitting the limit is abrupt and looks like a dependency outage.
- A flat open count well below max is the expected shape.

panels.title: OS Threads
panels.description:
- OS threads the Go runtime is holding.
- Grows with blocking syscalls, not with goroutines, so a bounded pool should keep this flat.
- A climb into the hundreds means something is blocking in syscalls or cgo — the runtime never releases threads once created.

panels.title: Process Uptime
panels.description:
- Seconds since process start, per pod.
- A sawtooth back to zero is a restart — cross-check Container Restarts below for the cause.
- Uptime shorter than typical batch duration means pods are cycled faster than batches can finish; expect Batches Abandoned to be non-zero.

panels.title: Container Restarts (1h increase)
panels.description:
- Restarts over the trailing hour, split per container so a sidecar restart is not read as a service restart.
- Any non-zero outside a deploy needs a reason: OOM kill, liveness probe failure, or a panic.
- A `knowledge-service-be-go` restart returns that pod's in-flight batches to JetStream for redelivery — correlate with Batches Abandoned on the Pipeline dashboard.
- A `knowledge-hub-be-go` sidecar restart instead breaks in-flight uploads: expect INGESTER_UPLOAD_FAILED retries rather than abandoned batches.

panels.title: Registrations (5m)
panels.description: Successful RegisterConnector calls in the last 5 minutes (increase on connector_registrations_total).

panels.title: gRPC Error Rate (5m)
panels.description: Fraction of gRPC calls returning a non-OK status code (code != 0).

panels.title: HTTP 5xx Rate (5m)
panels.description: Fraction of REST requests answered with a 5xx status.

panels.title: gRPC In Flight
panels.description: grpc_active_requests — unary calls currently executing inside the metrics interceptor.

panels.title: Registrations by Connector (5m increase)
panels.description: connector_registrations_total counts successful RegisterConnector calls. Connectors re-register on every startup, so steps here usually line up with connector rollouts.

panels.title: gRPC Request Rate by Status Code
panels.description: The `code` label is the numeric gRPC status (0 = OK). The `status` label carries the full formatted status string and is intentionally not used for grouping.

panels.title: gRPC Mean Duration by Method
panels.description: sum/count over the 5m window — unaffected by the coarse default histogram bucket boundaries, so it is the more trustworthy latency signal for sub-second calls.

targets.expr: sum by (method) (rate(grpc_request_duration_seconds_sum{job=~".*registration-service.*", namespace="default"}[5m])) / clamp_min(sum by (method) (rate(grpc_request_duration_seconds_count{job=~".*registration-service.*", namespace="default"}[5m])), 0.0001)

panels.title: HTTP Request Rate by Route
panels.description: Route is chi's matched pattern (e.g. /api/v1/connectors/{name}/config-schema). Requests matching no route collapse to "unmatched".

targets.expr: sum by (route) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_sum{job=~".*registration-service.*", namespace="default"}[5m])) / clamp_min(sum by (route) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count{job=~".*registration-service.*", namespace="default"}[5m])), 0.0001)

panels.title: HTTP Payload Throughput
panels.description: Bytes/s in and out, from the http_request_size_bytes / http_response_size_bytes histogram sums. Only non-zero-length bodies are recorded.

panels.title: GC Pause (max)
panels.description: Longest stop-the-world GC pause per pod. go_gc_duration_seconds is a Prometheus summary, not a histogram: there is no _bucket series, so histogram_quantile cannot be used here. The Go collector exposes quantiles 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 and 1 only — there is no 0.99. quantile="1" is the max pause over the runtime's buffer of recent GC cycles, so it reports the worst recent pause rather than a windowed percentile.

panels.title: Process Uptime
panels.description: Time since process start. A sawtooth here is a restart.

panels.title: Pods Up
panels.description: Single replica by design — SSE sessions are held in memory by the pod serving them.

panels.title: SSE Active Connections
panels.description: request_service_sse_active_connections — currently open Server-Sent Events result-push connections. This is the metric to scale on if the service ever needs more than one replica.

panels.title: Create Errors (5m)
panels.description: Connection-test jobs the service failed to create (outcome="error").

panels.title: Results Received (5m)
panels.description: Connection-test results consumed from NATS.

panels.title: Unmatched Results (5m)
panels.description: Results that could not be correlated back to a request (e.g. an empty job id). Sustained non-zero means result pushes are being dropped on the floor.

panels.title: Test Creation by Outcome (rate)
panels.description: request_service_connectiontest_requests_total — job-creation attempts, labelled created / error.

panels.title: Test Creation Error Ratio
panels.description: Share of creation attempts that failed before a job was queued.

panels.title: Created vs Results Received (rate)
panels.description: The two legs of the round trip. A persistent gap between created and results means jobs are queued but their results are not coming back over NATS.

panels.title: Results by Connect Outcome (rate)
panels.description: request_service_connectiontest_results_total — how the tested connection actually resolved (success / failure). This is the health of the target systems, not of this service.

panels.title: Unmatched Results (rate)
panels.description: Results dropped because they could not be correlated to an outstanding request.

panels.title: Round-Trip Duration (p50 / p95 / p99)
panels.description: request_service_connectiontest_duration_seconds — wall time from the job being created in the job engine to its result arriving over NATS. Derived from the stored request row's created_at, so it spans the whole round trip including the connector's own network connect, not just this service's work.

panels.title: Round-Trip p95 by Connector
panels.description: The same round trip split by connector. One slow connector shows up here without dragging the aggregate quantiles beside it.

panels.title: Round Trips Measured vs Results Received
panels.description: The histogram only observes results whose request row existed to measure against; a result whose request was never persisted is still stored, but cannot be timed. A persistent gap between these lines means creation-time persistence is failing — look for the 'no stored request to measure against' warning in the service log.

panels.title: In Flight / Stalled
panels.description: request_service_connectiontest_inflight — connection tests dispatched with no result recorded yet, read from the pending rows in Postgres at scrape time (so it survives a restart and does not depend on which replica dispatched the job). 'pending' is normal in-flight work and should return to zero between tests; 'stalled' has waited more than 10 minutes and is work the job engine almost certainly never returned. A rising stalled line is the signal the duration histogram cannot give you, because a round trip that never completes is never observed. Reported per pod, so this sums replicas rather than averaging them.

panels.title: SSE Connection Churn
panels.description: Rate of change of the open-connection gauge. Large symmetric swings mean clients are reconnecting rather than holding a stream.

panels.title: API Request Rate by Route
panels.description: Connect RPC traffic. The route label is the raw URL path, which for Connect is the fully-qualified procedure — a bounded set, so no cardinality risk. /metrics, /healthz and /ready are excluded: at a 30s scrape interval they would otherwise dominate the chart. /events is absent by design, since the SSE stream is deliberately left uninstrumented.

panels.title: API Duration p95 by Route
panels.description: The service opts into pipeline-lib-go's SubsecondLatencyBuckets for this histogram (0.005s-10s), so histogram_quantile is meaningful. The 10s ceiling fits because /events is excluded from instrumentation and every other route returns promptly — the connection test itself is dispatched asynchronously and its multi-minute round trip is measured separately by request_service_connectiontest_duration_seconds.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, route) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job=~".*request-service.*", namespace="default", route!~"/metrics|/healthz|/ready"}[5m])))

panels.title: HTTP In Flight
panels.description: http_active_requests carries no route or method labels, so this covers the whole instrumented surface including /metrics, /healthz and /ready — it cannot be filtered down to API routes. It should sit near zero: the SSE stream is excluded from instrumentation, so long-lived connections never accumulate here.

panels.title: API Payload Throughput
panels.description: Bytes/s in and out, from the http_request_size_bytes / http_response_size_bytes histogram sums. Only non-zero-length bodies are recorded. Throughput uses _sum, which is independent of bucket layout — worth knowing because the two histograms are bucketed differently: response size opts into BodySizeBuckets (256 B-64 MB), while request size is deliberately left on the SDK default, which is the finer of the two below 256 B and suits the small Connect messages and bare probes this service accepts. Size percentiles are therefore only meaningful on the response side. Health and scrape routes are excluded to match the other panels in this row.

panels.title: Goroutines
panels.description: Each open SSE stream holds goroutines; a rising floor that never comes back down alongside a flat connection gauge is a leak signal.

panels.title: GC Pause (max)
panels.description: Longest stop-the-world GC pause per pod. go_gc_duration_seconds is a Prometheus summary, not a histogram: there is no _bucket series, so histogram_quantile cannot be used here. The Go collector exposes quantiles 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 and 1 only — there is no 0.99. quantile="1" is the max pause over the runtime's buffer of recent GC cycles, so it reports the worst recent pause rather than a windowed percentile.

panels.title: Open vs Max FDs
panels.description: Long-lived SSE streams each hold a socket, so this is the ceiling that limits concurrent UI subscribers.

panels.title: Process Uptime
panels.description: Time since process start. A restart drops every in-memory SSE session, so sawtooth here explains client reconnect storms.

panels.title: HTTP Error Rates by Status Code

targets.expr: topk(10, sum by (message) (increase(log_messages_total{job="archiver", namespace="default", pod=~".*", level="error"}[5m])))
histogram_quantile(0.50, sum(rate(archiver_operation_duration_seconds_bucket{job="archiver", namespace="default", pod=~".*"}[5m])) by (le, pod, operation))
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(archiver_operation_duration_seconds_bucket{job="archiver", namespace="default", pod=~".*"}[5m])) by (le, pod, operation))
histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(archiver_operation_duration_seconds_bucket{job="archiver", namespace="default", pod=~".*"}[5m])) by (le, pod, operation))
